Is TypeScript catching up with JavaScript on GitHub?

Every chart and every number below is computed by code from one public file: GitHub Innovation Graph, data/languages.csv. The one exception is a statement quoted from GitHub's Octoverse report, attributed where it appears. Nothing here is advice.

Is TypeScript catching up with JavaScript on GitHub? As a share of JavaScript, yes, and quickly; in raw numbers, no: JavaScript's lead grew. Every quarter, GitHub counts the developers in each economy who push to repositories containing each language; a repository that holds both languages counts for both. We follow the 2 economies reported for both in every quarter.

In the first quarter of 2020, TypeScript had 38% as many pushers as JavaScript. By the first quarter of 2022, it had 81%. In raw numbers, though, JavaScript's lead grew, from 0.0 million to 0.0 million pushers, because both languages grew. GitHub's Octoverse 2025 report named TypeScript the most used language on GitHub in August 2025, by contributor counts. That is a different count from the quarterly pushers in this video.

Over the 2 years, TypeScript pushers grew 2.6 times over, and JavaScript pushers 1.2 times. Among the 2 languages with the most pushers, the fastest growing was TypeScript.

The ratio moved fastest in the last year: it rose 20 percentage points, against at most 24 percentage points in any earlier year.

Economy by economy, the picture is the same. TypeScript reached 50% of JavaScript's pushers in 1 of the 2 economies, up from 1 in 2020. The highest ratio was 107%.

Limits: GitHub omits economies with too few active developers; those reported for TypeScript rose from 3 to 3, hence the fixed set. Only public repositories count, developers can count under both, and location comes from IP addresses. The data shows how many pushed, not why. Source: GitHub's Innovation Graph, public domain.

How this page was made

The text was written by an AI system; every number in it is filled in from the computed figures above. The charts are drawn by code (matplotlib) from the data. The same analysis is also made as a video narrated by a synthetic voice (Kokoro text-to-speech), not a recording of any person.
